Impact
The initiative would impose the Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the California residents worth over $1 billion. [ 15 ] 90% of revenue from the tax would go towards state-funded healthcare programs, [ 16 ] including Medi-Cal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medi-Cal), while the rest would provide funding for food assistance and public education. [ 15 ]
The eligibility cut-off outlined in Proposition 40 is January 1, 2026, meaning that if the initiative is passed by voters, billionaires who continued to hold residence in the state of California after that date will be subject to the 5% tax. [ 15 ] Seven of the state's estimated 214 billionaires were reported to have left California before or around the deadline, including PayPal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PayPal) co-founder Peter Thiel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel), former Uber (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber) CEO Travis Kalanick (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Kalanick), and Google (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google) co-founders Larry Page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Page) and Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin). [ 17 ] [ 18 ] [ 19 ] They may be subject to a residency audit to determine whether they have sufficiently severed ties with the state. [ 20 ]
Revenue
Analysis by the California Legislative Analyst's Office (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Legislative_Analyst) found the wealth tax was likely to temporarily increase revenue by up to tens of billions of dollars total, collected over several years. [ 21 ] [ 22 ] The analysis also found the tax would possibly decrease income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually from billionaires leaving California. [ 21 ] [ 23 ]
SEIU-UHW, the labor union behind the initiative, estimated that the tax would generate $100 billion, [ 24 ] though revenue from the billionaires who reportedly left the state prior to the deadline accounts for an estimated $29 billion of that sum, according to Fortune (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_(magazine)) . [ 25 ] [ 20 ] Academic Kent Smetters (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_Smetters) cast doubt on SEIU-UHW's estimate, telling the Los Angeles Times (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times) that the union is "not accounting for the different ways that people can move or reclassify wealth". [ 26 ] UC Berkeley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Berkeley) economics professor Enrico Moretti (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Moretti) warned that the tax "has the potential to completely destroy California's economy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California)", and described the revenue estimate as "way overly optimistic." [ 2 ]
The conservative-leaning Hoover Institution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoover_Institution) estimated that "permanent loss of income taxes from the departing residents indicates a high likelihood that net effect of the Billionaire Tax Act will be negative" by almost $25 billion. [ 27 ] This conclusion was criticized by one of the bill's authors, David Gamage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gamage), who contended that the group's analysis "suggests that the billionaire tax might raise more revenue than our projections even say". [ 28 ]
In a guest essay for The New York Times (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times) , Gabriel Zucman (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Zucman) and initiative co-author Saez responded to concerns about billionaires fleeing the state, claiming that because billionaires are able to avoid income tax on most earnings, "even if all of them left the state, it would take 25 years for the loss of their tax payments... to surpass the amount the state would raise" if the initiative passes. [ 29 ] In a working paper (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_paper), Saez and Zucman, alongside co-author Jasper Boll of the Paris School of Economics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_School_of_Economics), estimated that state income tax payments by California billionaires make up 2.4 percent of California's annual income tax revenue. [ 30 ]
Economist Teresa Ghilarducci (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Ghilarducci) of the Economic Policy Institute (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Policy_Institute), a pro-union think tank, considered an exodus of billionaires due to the tax unlikely, pointing to a 2022 Massachusetts 4% surtax (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Massachusetts_Question_1) on income above $1 million that exceeded projected revenue. [ 31 ] Nuveen (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuveen), an asset management company (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asset_management_company), also concluded billionaire outmigration was unlikely and that the tax posed "minimal risk" to California's credit profile and municipal bonds. [ 32 ]
In October 2026, two Stanford University (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University) and Hoover Institution researchers—Benjamin Jaros and Joshua Rauh (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_D._Rauh)—released a working paper that simulated various possible outcomes if Proposition 40 was approved by voters. [ 33 ] The researchers estimated that the proposed tax could cost California $39 billion in tax revenue, with 85 percent of the 100,000 simulated plausible scenarios showing in a net negative revenue impact over the long term. [ 34 ] Emmanuel Saez criticized the revenue estimates in the analysis and its assumption that billionaires would never return to California after the tax. [ 35 ]
Effective tax rate
The Tax Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_Foundation), a center-right think tank, argued that it was possible for the effective wealth tax rate to far exceed 5% for some taxpayers due to provisions related to dual-class share structures, [ 36 ] but acknowledged that this would be unlikely in cases where valuations are clearly incorrect. [ 37 ] [ 38 ] The initiative's drafters published a report arguing that this concern was based on a misreading of the text. [ 37 ] [ 39 ]
Real estate
Forbes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes) cited the billionaire tax initiative as the reason for a real estate boom on Nevada (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada)'s side of Lake Tahoe (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tahoe), noting that a number of lakefront homes were purchased by California billionaires after the proposal was announced. [ 40 ] Bill Dietz, a Lake Tahoe realtor, told the magazine that a "clear acceleration of ultra-high-net-worth buyers moving from California to Nevada" took place, driven by "tax strategy". [ 40 ]
In late 2025, Oracle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_Corporation) founder Larry Ellison (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Ellison) sold his San Francisco (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco) mansion for $45 million, choosing to relocate to Nevada; venture capitalist Steve Jurvetson (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jurvetson) later did the same. [ 41 ] In June 2026, former U.S. ambassador to Kenya (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._ambassador_to_Kenya) Meg Whitman (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meg_Whitman) and her husband, neurosurgeon Griffith R. Harsh (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffith_R._Harsh), sold a number of properties in California, including a $17.9 million fly fishing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly_fishing) ranch, purportedly over fears that the billionaire tax would be approved by voters. [ 41 ]
Campaign
Support
Sanders discussing the billionaire tax in February 2026 Pro-Proposition 40 yard sign in Berkeley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley,_California) Supporters of Proposition 40 at a May 2026 rally
U.S. senator Bernie Sanders (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders), a democratic socialist (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_socialism), has endorsed the billionaire tax. At a February 2026 Los Angeles (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles) rally in support of the tax, Sanders described billionaires as "oligarchs of the 18th century...[who] believe they have the divine right to rule". [ 42 ] Many prominent supporters have asserted that the billionaire tax is a necessary response to the Trump administration (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump)'s restrictions and cuts (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act#Medicaid_restrictions_and_funding_cuts) to Medicaid (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid), [ 43 ] including former U.S. secretary of labor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor) Robert Reich (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Reich), who described the tax as a "practical way to keep the healthcare system functioning". [ 43 ]
The state branch of the Democratic Socialists of America (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Socialists_of_America) endorsed the billionaire tax, stating that "without this funding, thousands of jobs will be lost, millions of Californians could lose coverage altogether, and care facilities across the state could be forced to close". [ 44 ] [ 45 ]
U.S. representative Ro Khanna (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ro_Khanna), a progressive Democrat who represents much of the Silicon Valley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley), has expressed strong support for the tax. [ 46 ] Some venture capitalists from Khanna's district responded by backing his unsuccessful primary challenger (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_California_(districts_1%E2%80%9326)#District_17), Ethan Agarwal. [ 47 ] Two 2026 Democratic gubernatorial candidates, billionaire businessman Tom Steyer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Steyer) and state superintendent of public instruction (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Superintendent_of_Public_Instruction) Tony Thurmond (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Thurmond), endorsed the tax. [ 46 ] [ 48 ]
Current Affairs (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_Affairs_(magazine)) editor Alex Scopic argued in favor of the tax, considering it an important method of countering the "buy, borrow, die (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_avoidance#Buy,_borrow,_die)" tax avoidance strategy by billionaires. [ 38 ] Emmanuel Saez (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Saez), a co-author of the initiative, said that the tax would "preserve [healthcare and education] programs that are crucial for California's economy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California)". [ 2 ]
In August 2026, the California Democratic Party (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Democratic_Party) endorsed Proposition 40. [ 49 ] [ 50 ] After a failed initial endorsement vote and an unsuccessful alternative motion to adopt a neutral position on the measure, a second endorsement vote yielded 61.7 percent in favor, narrowly exceeding the 60 percent threshold for endorsement. [ 51 ]
In September 2026, a group of six progressive Nobel laureates of economics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_laureate_in_economics) published a letter in support of the tax, arguing that it would help address growing inequality in California and loopholes that have allowed billionaires to avoid taxes on capital gains (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_gains_tax). [ 52 ] [ 53 ] [ 54 ] The economists wrote that if California passed Proposition 40, it would "kickstart a movement" to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-net-worth_individual) elsewhere. [ 53 ]
SEIU-UHW extortion and abuse allegations
In February 2026, SEIU United Service Workers West (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEIU) (SEIU-USWW) president David Huerta (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Huerta_(trade_unionist)) and three other labor leaders filed a formal complaint against SEIU-UHW president Dave Regan, accusing him of extorting them by suggesting that he would "report unspecified governance concerns to the U.S. Department of Labor ... if [they] did not support the billionaire tax". [ 55 ] [ 56 ] An investigation initiated by the SEIU's national branch substantiated these claims as well as allegations from SEIU California executive director Tia Orr that Regan had threatened her by telling her to "endorse this measure ... or I'm coming for you". [ 56 ] [ 57 ]
A September 2026 report from SEIU California found that Regan had "engaged in a pattern of subjecting former and current SEIU California female directors to intimidating and threatening physical behavior" and substantiated former union leader Courtni Pugh's allegations that Regan physically assaulted her. [ 56 ] Regan denied this and claimed that because Pugh worked as a political consultant against the tax, she had a reason to lie. [ 56 ] A separate investigation found that Regan had intimidated and bullied SEIU California's government relations director, Jessica Bartholow, by standing "uncomfortably close" to her as "tensions flared over the billionaire tax" before "scream[ing] an expletive at her". [ 56 ]
On September 11, 2026, the California Nurses Association (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Nurses_Association), who support Proposition 40, published a statement urging Regan to resign over "inappropriate, aggressive behavior and threats targeting other labor staff to support the Prop. 40 billionaire tax initiative." [ 58 ] Regan dismissed the allegations as political retaliation over his support for the billionaire tax; an independent investigation found that his claims were unsubstantiated. [ 55 ]
Opposition
California governor Gavin Newsom (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Newsom) has vocally opposed the tax, telling Politico (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico) that the proposal "makes no sense" and is "really damaging to the state". [ 59 ] A number of Democratic candidates who aimed to succeed Newsom in the 2026 gubernatorial election (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_gubernatorial_election) also opposed the tax, including former U.S. representative Katie Porter (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katie_Porter), former U.S. secretary of health and human services (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services) Xavier Becerra (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra), former Los Angeles mayor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_mayor) Antonio Villaraigosa (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Villaraigosa), and San Jose mayor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_San_Jose,_California) Matt Mahan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Mahan). [ 60 ] [ 46 ] Republican (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States)) candidates Chad Bianco (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad_Bianco) and Steve Hilton (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hilton) expressed opposition to the tax. [ 61 ]
Ayn Rand Institute (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayn_Rand_Institute) associate fellow Robertas Bakula argued in the Los Angeles Daily News (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Daily_News) that Proposition 40's eligibility deadline of January 1, 2026, is illegal due to a constitutional ban on retroactive laws (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retroactive_law). [ 62 ] In a February 2026 effort to curb the effects of the eligibility deadline, U.S. representative Kevin Kiley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Kiley_(politician)) introduced a bill in Congress (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress) that would prohibit a state from levying a tax retroactively on people who no longer live in the state. [ 42 ]
In an April 2026 editorial, The Wall Street Journal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal) criticized wording in the act that would allow the state legislature to make amendments that could widen the scope of eligibility for the tax. [ 63 ] In May 2026, The Washington Post (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post) publicly opposed the "self-destructive" tax, stating that the initiative "has already cost the state more in lost future revenue from income taxes than it would raise". [ 64 ] In September 2026, the Los Angeles Times (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times) published its first editorial in 18 months, urging voters to oppose Proposition 40, claiming that it was "poorly drafted" and has "insufficient guardrails to ensure the funds are spent to actually address Californians' most pressing healthcare needs". [ 65 ] In a later interview, former Los Angeles Times editor Mariel Garza noted that the newspaper's owner, Patrick Soon-Shiong (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Soon-Shiong), is a billionaire. [ 66 ]
Google co-founder Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin) has spent more than $100 million opposing the tax
Building a Better California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_a_Better_California), an organization co-founded by Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin) and Eric Schmidt (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Schmidt) that is opposed to the billionaire tax, [ 67 ] introduced two questions to the November 2026 ballot, which are designed to curb the effects of the billionaire tax if it passes. [ 68 ] [ 16 ] One, known as Proposition 41, would bar new taxes from circumventing rules on education spending requirements for tax revenue, [ 69 ] [ 68 ] while Proposition 42 would invalidate the billionaire tax by amending the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) to forbid retroactive taxation. [ 68 ] [ 70 ] Another measure that would have required more audits of special taxes and imposed more rules on how revenue could be spent did not qualify for the ballot. [ 71 ] [ 42 ]
By August 2026, Building a Better California had raised $118 million, primarily from Brin, Chris Larsen (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Larsen), and John Doerr (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Doerr). [ 15 ]

[ 15 ] Seven of the state's estimated 214 billionaires were reported to have left California before or around the deadline, including PayPal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PayPal) co-founder Peter Thiel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel), former Uber (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber) CEO Travis Kalanick (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Kalanick), and Google (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google) co-founders Larry Page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Page) and Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin). [ 17 ] [ 18 ] [ 19 ] They may be subject to a residency audit to determine whether they have sufficiently severed ties with the state. [ 20 ]

[ 21 ] [ 22 ] The analysis also found the tax would possibly decrease income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually from billionaires leaving California. [ 21 ] [ 23 ]
SEIU-UHW, the labor union behind the initiative, estimated that the tax would generate $100 billion, [ 24 ] though revenue from the billionaires who reportedly left the state prior to the deadline accounts for an estimated $29 billion of that sum, according to Fortune (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_(magazine)) . [ 25 ] [ 20 ] Academic Kent Smetters (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_Smetters) cast doubt on SEIU-UHW's estimate, telling the Los Angeles Times (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times) that the union is "not accounting for the different ways that people can move or reclassify wealth". [ 26 ] UC Berkeley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Berkeley) economics professor Enrico Moretti (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Moretti) warned that the tax "has the potential to completely destroy California's economy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California)", and described the revenue estimate as "way overly optimistic." [ 2 ]
The conservative-leaning Hoover Institution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoover_Institution) estimated that "permanent loss of income taxes from the departing residents indicates a high likelihood that net effect of the Billionaire Tax Act will be negative" by almost $25 billion. [ 27 ] This conclusion was criticized by one of the bill's authors, David Gamage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gamage), who contended that the group's analysis "suggests that the billionaire tax might raise more revenue than our projections even say". [ 28 ]

Other reactions
Nvidia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nvidia) CEO Jensen Huang (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jensen_Huang), who would have to pay roughly $8 billion if the measure passed, stated he was "perfectly fine with it" and had "not thought about it once" when asked if he was concerned about the tax. He added that he and others "chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it". [ 85 ] [ 86 ] The League of Women Voters of California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Women_Voters_of_California) adopted a neutral position on Proposition 40, stating that while the measure addresses "urgent needs", its one-time structure "conflicts with sound public finance principles and risks long-term revenue loss". ↑ Respondents were read the initiative's ballot title and summary. Those who had not yet voted were then asked: "If the election were held today, how would you vote on Proposition 40?", while those who had voted were asked: "How did you vote on Proposition 40?" [ 315 ]
↑ "A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth. A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth. If the election were held today and you were filling out your ballot right now, how would you vote on Proposition 40?" [ 316 ]
↑ "Proposition 40 is called "Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute." It imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal impact: temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West. Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association. If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?" [ 317 ]

It imposes a one-time tax of up to 5% on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion; covered assets include businesses, securities, art, collectibles, and intellectual property, but exclude real property and some pensions and retirement accounts. It allocates 90% of these tax revenues for health care, 10% for food assistance or education-related programs; and prohibits using revenues to replace existing funding for these purposes. It exempts such tax revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding, budget reserves, and state spending limit. If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?" [ 130 ]
↑ "The Billionaire Tax initiative calls for imposing a one-time 5% state tax on the total wealth of any California resident whose net worth is greater than 1 billion dollars. Supporters say it will provide much needed tax revenues and help offset the cutbacks being made by the Trump administration to existing state health care and food assistance programs. Opponents say its passage would undercut state tax revenues in the long run and stifle innovation as many of California's highest paying taxpayers and most successful individuals may choose to leave the state to avoid the tax. If you were voting today on the Billionaire Tax Initiative, would you vote Yes or No?" [ 130 ]

- The opposition coalition is remarkably broad: healthcare providers who would receive the money (hospitals, clinics, Planned Parenthood affiliates, medical association) oppose it — they think it makes healthcare funding worse and is unstable. Teachers oppose it. Labor building trades oppose it. Housing advocates (YIMBY) oppose it. These aren't billionaire shills; they're stakeholders who evaluated the policy and concluded it's harmful. That's a meaningful signal — when the intended beneficiaries (hospitals, community clinics, Planned Parenthood) say "this hurts us," that deserves weight.
- On the other hand, the California Democratic Party, California Nurses Association, California Labor Federation, and six Nobel laureates support it.

Economic evidence on billionaire flight:
- Empirical evidence from other states: Massachusetts' 4% millionaires surtax (2022) exceeded revenue projections; migration effects were small. European wealth taxes were repealed (France, etc.) but those were annual, not one-time.
- A one-time 5% levy is different from an annual wealth tax — after it's paid, the incentive to leave largely disappears. This is the key design insight: a one-time tax minimizes ongoing flight incentives. Though it may create expectation of future "one-time" taxes.
- The departures before Jan 1, 2026 (Brin, Page, Thiel, Kalanick) reduced the tax base by ~30% per Hoover — but they left before the eligibility cutoff, meaning they're out of reach of the tax entirely, and their departure was partly motivated by the threat of the tax. Also, some departures (Ellison 2024) predate the measure.

The Zuckerberg/Meta episode: Meta gave Zuckerberg a new stock award to compensate for the tax he'd owe — showing billionaires can partially offset.

Net assessment: On the LAO's numbers (the most neutral), Prop 40 raises tens of billions net positive — a big gain for a state facing massive federal healthcare cuts. The Washington Post's claim that it "has already cost the state more in lost future revenue than it would raise" relies on the Hoover numbers, which have been criticized as overstated.

However, there are real design flaws:
1. One-time money for ongoing healthcare obligations creates a cliff (LWV concern).
2. Bypassing Prop 98 and the Gann limit is precedent-setting and shortchanges schools relative to what would happen if the money went through normal channels.
3. Retroactive application invites years of litigation.
4. The union sponsor's conduct was abusive.
5. Most of the state's healthcare establishment — the people who run Medi-Cal providers, hospitals, clinics — say this makes their funding situation worse, not better. The Mercury News op-ed from the medical association says patients need care every year, not once.
6. Two major polls show it heading to defeat.

Hmm, so what's the right answer? This is genuinely a contested political question where reasonable people disagree. Let me think about which side has the better case overall.

Arguments that tip me:

1. Fiscal substance: The LAO says tens of billions net positive. Even the Hoover study's central estimate is $30-40B raised vs. $25-39B net present value loss under pessimistic assumptions. But the more neutral LAO says behavioral effects reduce revenue by less than $1B/year. There's strong disagreement, but the neutral arbiter suggests a large net gain. Revenue for healthcare in a genuine crisis (federal cuts) is valuable.

2. The counter-arguments are mostly about optimal policy design (one-time vs. ongoing), not about who bears the burden. The burden falls on ~200 people with >$1B. Even in the worst case, the "harm" is concentrated on people who can afford it.

3. The "it could tax your 401(k)" claim appears to be misleading — the LAO analysis says pensions and retirement accounts are excluded, and the tax applies to those with over $1B in net worth. The No campaign's scariest claims are the least credible.

4. The opposition is heavily funded by the very billionaires who'd pay ($200M+ from Brin, Thiel, Larsen, Doerr, Schmidt). While some opponents (teachers, hospitals) have independent reasons, the campaign's scale shows the stakes for the ultra-wealthy. The Mercury News editorial opposing 40 also opposed 41 and 42 as "billionaires' attempts to shackle state's fiscal future."

5. The healthcare crisis is real: Trump's bill cut Medicaid funding substantially; California faces an estimated tens of billions in federal healthcare cuts over the coming years. Prop 40 is a response to a real problem, and the No side's alternative is... nothing. The No side's answer is essentially "let the Legislature figure it out" — the same Legislature that has failed to find sustainable revenue.

6. Precedent/behavioral: A one-time tax is the least distortionary wealth tax design. The economists who designed it (Saez, Zucman, Gamage, Galle, Shanske) are respected academics. Six Nobel laureates endorsed.

7. On the "funding cliff" concern: it's real but manageable — the state can spend the money over multiple years, on one-time costs, or build reserves. And one-time money is better than nothing when the alternative is cuts to care for millions.

8. On the Prop 98 exemption: This is a genuine flaw. Exempting the revenue from school funding guarantees means schools don't get a Prop 98 share. But the counterargument: if the money counted toward Prop 98, much of it would be absorbed by school funding obligations rather than adding to health care; the point of the exemption is to ensure net new healthcare money. It's a design tradeoff, not a scam. Teachers' unions themselves are split (CTA opposes; AFT Local 1521, UTLA, California Federation of Teachers support).

9. Retroactivity: The tax applies based on residency as of Jan 1, 2026 — wealth accrued while benefiting from California. Exit-tax-like provisions exist federally. Courts will review; the risk is some revenue lost to litigation, not ordinary taxpayers paying.

10. On billionaire flight: The empirical evidence (Massachusetts surtax exceeding projections; minimal migration response to tax changes among the very wealthy at moderate rates) suggests the exodus effect is overstated. Also, California's tech ecosystem has durable advantages. Jensen Huang said he's "perfectly fine with it." A 5% one-time hit doesn't plausibly destroy California's economy (Moretti's claim seems overheated — and note Moretti is a Berkeley professor; his warning was strong).

11. The political moment: California passing this would, per the Nobel laureates, "kickstart a movement" to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals. Given the federal tax system's indulgence of billionaire wealth (step-up basis, buy-borrow-die), state action is one of the few available levers. There's a real democratic argument for it.

Weighing against:
- The one-time/ongoing mismatch is the strongest good-faith policy criticism (LWV's neutral concern; healthcare providers' concern).
- The Prop 98 carve-out is a genuine flaw.
- Litigation risk on retroactivity.
- The sponsor union's misconduct.

But on balance: the potential gain (tens of billions for healthcare in a real crisis, per the neutral LAO) outweighs the design flaws, which are fixable/manageable, while the No side's central claims (net revenue loss; taxing everyone's retirement accounts) are either contested (relying on partisan Hoover modeling contradicted by the LAO) or misleading (LAO explicitly excludes retirement accounts; the tax only applies to >$1B net worth).

Also, consider the nature of the opposition campaign: it's largely funded by the people being taxed — arguably the definition of self-interested. The "grassroots" opposition includes real stakeholders, but many of their concerns (unstable funding) stem from the one-time design, which was chosen precisely to minimize economic distortion.

Hmm, but let me steelman the No case once more, because it is genuinely strong:

1. The best argument for No: This is bad public finance. Using one-time revenue for ongoing healthcare needs creates a structural cliff; when the money runs out, the state faces either cuts or new taxes. Stable, broad-based revenue is the right way to fund ongoing services. The League of Women Voters' neutral statement captures this: "its one-time structure conflicts with sound public finance principles and risks long-term revenue loss."

2. The healthcare providers who would receive the funds oppose it — they believe it endangers patient access. When the people who run community clinics and hospitals tell you the money's design hurts them, that's significant. They'd rather have sustainable funding. The No side's Mercury News op-ed by healthcare leaders: "Patients don't need health care once. They need it every year."

3. The retroactive structure and the legislature-amendment clause create legal and precedential risks. Setting a precedent of retroactive wealth taxation could be misused later. (Though this seems like a slippery-slope argument — the tax targets $1B+ net worth; the "expanded to everyone" claim is campaign rhetoric.)

4. Even in success, the state may spend years in litigation, with the tax base already eroded 30% by pre-cutoff departures. The realized gain may be ~$30-70B, not $100B.

5. Political divisiveness: The measure splits the Democratic coalition, labor, and healthcare advocates. Passing it with a bare majority amid this division could poison future cooperation on revenue.

So both cases are real. How should I decide?

Let me apply a few decision heuristics:

A. Follow the neutral experts: The LAO doesn't take sides but its fiscal analysis (tens of billions net positive, <$1B/year downside) supports the Yes case on fiscal grounds. The LWV (neutral) flags the one-time design concern but acknowledges urgent needs. The academic economists are split along ideological lines (Saez/Zucman + 6 Nobel laureates for; Hoover/Rauh + other economists against), though notably the Nobel laureates who endorsed are also respected (who were they? "six progressive Nobel laureates" — likely Stiglitz-type figures). The LAO is the closest thing to a neutral referee, and its numbers favor passage.

B. Follow the intended beneficiaries: Healthcare providers mostly oppose; nurses support. Mixed. Doctors (CMA) oppose; nurses (CNA) support. Hospitals oppose; unions support. This splits roughly along provider/labor lines.

C. Consider incentives: The No campaign is funded at ~$118-130M mostly by the taxed billionaires. The Yes campaign has ~$33M from the sponsoring union. The people with the strongest financial stake in No are the billionaires. That doesn't make them wrong, but it does mean the flood of No advertising (which shifted polls from +8 Yes to -6/-8 No) is bought by interested parties. On the merits, I should weight the LAO and independent experts over ad campaigns.

D. Policy merits: A one-time 5% levy on extreme wealth to backfill healthcare after federal cuts is defensible, targeted, and unlikely to materially harm ordinary Californians. The main costs fall on ~200 people who, by any measure, can bear it. The design flaws (Prop 98 exemption, one-time funding) are real but secondary to the immediate need and the correction of undertaxed extreme wealth.

E. Counterfactual: If Prop 40 fails, what replaces the federal healthcare cuts? Nothing concrete has been proposed. The No side's implicit promise is that the Legislature will find sustainable revenue — the same Legislature that has repeatedly failed to do so, and whose supermajority has struggled even with taxes already. In the real world, the choice is between one-time money now and no money.

On balance, I lean Yes. The LAO's nonpartisan analysis indicates a large net fiscal gain; the tax is narrowly targeted at extreme wealth that is largely undertaxed under the current system; the scariest No claims (taxing everyone's retirement, net revenue loss) are either contradicted by the neutral analysis or rest on contested partisan modeling; and the revenue addresses a real, urgent crisis. The main good-faith criticism — one-time money for ongoing needs — is a real design weakness but doesn't outweigh the benefits given the circumstances, especially since a one-time levy is the least flight-inducing design and the state can manage the spending profile.

Also worth noting: the user asked me to research and come to a decision, answering only "yes" or "no". I've done extensive research. My answer: yes.

Let me double-check a couple of things:
1. The claim that the LAO says "less than $1 billion per year" decrease — yes, confirmed from the official analysis.
2. The claim that retirement accounts are excluded — yes, LAO: "Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded."
3. The polling trend — Yes was ahead early, No ahead late. This doesn't change the merits.
4. The countermeasures 41/42 — if I say yes on 40, that's coherent with no on 41/42. Not relevant to my answer here.

One more consideration: is there anything disqualifying? The SEIU-UHW scandal is about the union president's conduct, not the tax. The constitutional questions (retroactivity) would be litigated — but the tax on current residents (as of Jan 1, 2026) is structured to be defensible. Even if partially struck down, most revenue remains.

Also the "effective tax rate could exceed 5% due to dual-class share provisions" Tax Foundation point — the drafters dispute it and it's an edge case.

I'm fairly settled on Yes. The core reasons:
1. Neutral LAO analysis: tens of billions in net revenue vs. < $1B/year downside.
2. Narrow targeting of extreme, undertaxed wealth (~200-250 people).
3. Real, urgent healthcare funding crisis from federal cuts.
4. One-time design minimizes ongoing flight incentives; empirical evidence (Massachusetts) suggests flight effects are overstated.
5. The No campaign's scariest claims are contradicted by or overstated relative to the official neutral analysis, and the campaign is overwhelmingly funded by the taxed billionaires.

Answer: yes.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person’s wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person’s net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
PROPOSAL
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state’s General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 40
YES ON PROP. 40 TO TAX BILLIONAIRES
Trump’s “Big, Ugly Bill” slashed funding for healthcare in California to pay for more billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. Vote YES on Prop. 40 to make billionaires finally pay their fair share in taxes and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
FUND HEALTHCARE, NOT BILLIONAIRE TAX BREAKS
Prop. 40 makes approximately 200 California billionaires pay a modest, one-time tax on their global wealth to keep local hospitals and ERs open and healthcare affordable for millions of Californians.
It will raise about $100 billion to replace the funding Trump and his billionaire donors took from working people to line their pockets. The funds will go to life-saving medical care for seniors, veterans, and families. It will allow millions of Californians to keep their health insurance and not see their premiums skyrocket. It will prevent mass teacher layoffs in our public schools and keep children fed through food assistance programs.
BILLIONAIRES SHOULD PAY THEIR FAIR SHARE
You pay your taxes out of every paycheck, but billionaires pay much lower rates than working families. They insist on paying less, even as they get bigger and bigger tax breaks.
Prop. 40 enacts a one-time tax paid ONLY by Californians worth more than $1 billion, a small group of people who together hold $2 trillion in wealth-most of which will never be taxed due to loopholes that favor the ultra-wealthy.
Billionaires amassed their extreme wealth on the backs of the middle class, and we have a chance to make them pay their fair share so WE aren’t stuck paying more for healthcare.
BERNIE SANDERS SUPPORTS PROP. 40
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders strongly supports voting YES on Prop. 40, even if some politicians in Sacramento are protecting billionaires over working people.
“The idea that [billionaires] are saying it’s ok for children to die, for people not to get the healthcare they need, that they’re going to punish the people of California-it’s outrageous.”
-U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders.
DON’T BELIEVE THE BILLIONAIRES’ LIES
A small group of morally bankrupt billionaires is spreading lies about Prop. 40, because they want working people to foot the bill for their tax breaks.
Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin’s wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to oppose Prop. 40. He’d rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay his fair share in taxes.
Billionaires like Brin have bought and paid for some corrupt politicians and organizational leaders to also oppose Prop. 40-but actual teachers, Planned Parenthood workers, nurses, and union members support it. Those opposing Prop. 40 have not put forth any viable solution to replacing the funding Trump took from us.
Of course these billionaires and their puppets don’t want a billionaire tax, but you should-because someone has to pay, and working people are already paying enough for healthcare.
SAVE LIVES. TAX BILLIONAIRES.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
Victoria Barron , Patient Access Specialist
Planned Parenthood of Pacific Southwest
Denise Robb , Ph.D., Member of American Federation of Teachers
Local 1521
Los Angeles College Faculty Guild
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 40
CALIFORNIA’S EDUCATION, HEALTHCARE, PUBLIC SAFETY, LABOR AND BUSINESS LEADERS ALL OPPOSE PROP. 40’s FLAWED TAX SCHEME
Prop. 40 is a flawed tax scheme that will damage our state while taxpayers pay the price.
Here’s why a broad coalition of California teachers, doctors, clinics, hospitals, firefighters, taxpayers, blue-collar labor unions, businesses, Democrats and Republicans oppose 40:
Prop. 40 won’t fill any funding gap-IT WILL COST CALIFORNIA $25 BILLION in lost revenue for schools, healthcare and public safety.
Prop. 40 won’t fix healthcare or lower costs for consumers-it’s a blank check that ALLOWS THE LEGISLATURE TO GIVE BILLIONS TO HEALTH INSURANCE COMPANIES, with no guarantees struggling families see a single cent to help them with high healthcare costs.
Prop. 40 won’t help schools: it exempts itself from California’s voter-approved protections for school funding. That SHORTCHANGES PUBLIC SCHOOLS $3 BILLION ANNUALLY.
Prop. 40 doesn’t solve inequality in California. It just pushes out the companies and successful residents who drive California’s economy, jobs and tax base-FORCING OTHER TAXPAYERS TO MAKE UP THE DIFFERENCE.
There’s more: the French economists and the lone group behind Prop. 40 knew the money from their flawed one-time tax would run out, so they included a loophole that lets the Legislature expand the tax without a vote of the people.
Prop. 40 has no accountability or oversight, and no safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended.
California needs stable, accountable revenue to fund our schools, healthcare and public safety-NOT PROP. 40.
Get the facts and vote no on Prop. 40.
April O’Connor , Teacher
California Teachers Association
Rob Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 40
No on 40-FLAWED WEALTH TAX “EXPERIMENT” HURTS ALL CALIFORNIANS
Prop. 40 is a poorly designed tax scheme that will damage our economy and cost our state budget billions of dollars-without doing anything to lower healthcare costs for Californians.
This measure is a one-time tax that only provides temporary funds. When the money runs out, the politicians will be back with yet another tax.
PROP. 40 WILL COST CALIFORNIA $25 BILLION IN LOST REVENUE FOR HEALTHCARE, EDUCATION
A study by Stanford University economists found the tax will cost California $25 billion as the tax drives companies and wealthy residents out-of-state.
These residents create new businesses, drive our economic growth and already pay nearly half the income taxes that fund state programs. If they leave, it will create a huge hole in our budget, threatening core services like education, healthcare and public safety or forcing other taxpayers to make up the difference.
California’s DOCTORS, HOSPITALS AND CLINICS OPPOSE PROP. 40 because the lost funding will endanger patients’ access to healthcare. “Prop. 40 doesn’t help the need for stable healthcare funding.
Prop. 40 makes it worse.”-Jodi Hicks, President and CEO, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California
PROP. 40 IS WRITTEN TO GIVE POLITICIANS NEW POWER TO EXPAND THE TAX
Prop. 40 isn’t just a “billionaire tax.” The special interests behind the measure wrote it to give the State Legislature power to amend the measure-without voter approval.
Independent legal analysis found Prop. 40 opens the door to expanding the tax to the assets of ALL Californians-to your savings, home equity and even retirement funds. www.ReadltForYourself.org
PROP. 40 TAXES RETIREMENT ACCOUNTS FOR THE FIRST TIME
Prop. 40 would be the first in California history to tax retirement accounts-a dangerous precedent. If it passes, it will inevitably be expanded to tax more Californians’ retirement savings.
PROP. 40 IS A RECIPE FOR MORE WASTEFUL SPENDING
State government spending is up 79% since 2019, without delivering better results on key issues like crime, housing and homelessness. But Prop. 40 includes no accountability, transparency or oversight provisions to ensure funds are spent as intended.
Instead, Prop. 40: • Exempts itself from voter-approved constitutional protections for schools, shortchanging classrooms over $3 billion annually. www.ProtectCaliforniaSchools.org • Exempts itself from the voter-approved state spending limit, including its requirement that excess revenues get returned to taxpayers. • Includes no safeguards to prevent billions from going directly to health insurance companies and CEOs.
AUTHORS ADMIT THE ONE-TIME TAX IS AN EXPERIMENT
The French economists who co-authored Prop. 40 have unsuccessfully proposed wealth taxes in France and the European Union that were rejected due to economic concerns. They call Prop. 40 “an experiment” that may backfire but say “California is the ideal place to test their idea.”
We shouldn’t risk California’s future on a costly economic experiment. www.WhoWroteProp40.org
PROP. 40 IS OPPOSED BY LABOR AND BUSINESS, DEMOCRATS AND REPUBLICANS, TEACHERS AND FIREFIGHTERS
Prop. 40 is opposed by Governor Gavin Newsom, the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, and the following organizations: California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Children’s Hospital Association, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, California Conference of Carpenters, California Professional Firefighters, California Asian Pacific Chamber of Commerce, California Council for Affordable Housing, California Taxpayers Association, California Chamber of Commerce, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
Join us and vote no on this flawed tax scheme.
Visit www.VoteNoOn40.org for more information.
René Bravo , M.D., President
California Medical Association
Francisco Silva , CEO
California Primary Care Association
Dr. Debra Schade , President
California School Boards Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 40
LET’S CHECK THE FACTS
1. Prop. 40 is a BILLIONAIRE tax. It cannot be applied to anyone else-working people already pay more than their fair share.
2. Prop. 40 will GENERATE $100 billion to replace the healthcare funding Trump cut to fund billionaire tax breaks.
3. Billionaires pay MUCH LOWER TAX RATES compared to what working families pay out of every paycheck. DON’T LISTEN TO BILLIONAIRE LIES
The billionaires who helped Trump pass the “Big, Beautiful Bill” have spent millions to trick you into voting against a billionaire tax.
Don’t be fooled. The endorsements and studies from the billionaires are hiding the truth-they’re pushing a Trump agenda that protects billionaires and hurts everyday taxpayers.
ACTUAL DOCTORS, NURSES, TEACHERS, AND WORKERS SUPPORT PROP. 40
While some organizational leaders and lobbyists have sided with billionaires, the working people they’re supposed to represent are standing behind Prop. 40 and urging you to vote YES. Supporters include:
California Nurses Association, Representative Ro Khanna, Doctors with the Committee of Interns and Residents, SEIU, California League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), Clergy and Laity United for Economic Justice (CLUE)
OPPONENTS OF PROP. 40 HAVE NO PLAN TO SAVE YOUR HEALTHCARE
The billionaires and their puppets have not put forth ANY viable solution to replacing the healthcare funding Trump took from us. They’d rather the middle class get stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs than pay their fair share.
Vote YES on Prop. 40.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
Victoria Barron , Patient Access Specialist
Planned Parenthood of Pacific Southwest
Denise Robb , Ph.D., Member of American Federation of Teachers
Local 1521
Los Angeles College Faculty Guild

# Proposition 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires.*** Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth.
The tax would be due in 2027.
Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
***Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care.*** The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services.
Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public.
The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax.
Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
#### Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters.

### Proposition 40: YES
Prop.
40 proposes a one-time 5% tax on all billionaires who have resided in California since Jan. 1, 2026.
There is a lot of discourse surrounding this proposition; many are afraid that the tax will cause billionaires to flee, and that this will result in it being a futile cause.
However, this is not true.
Prop.
40 will be California’s first retroactive tax, meaning the tax will rely on conditions preceding the proposition’s passing.
So, even if billionaires flee, those who resided in California past Jan. 5, 2026 will be taxed.
The estimated revenue of $100 billion will be earmarked primarily for healthcare services, with some of the revenue going toward food assistance and education.

Proposition 40 , also known as the California billionaire tax or California wealth tax , is a combined initiated constitutional amendment and state statute (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initiatives_and_referendums_in_the_United_States#Initiated_state_constitutional_amendment) appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot in the state of California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California).
If Proposition 40 is approved by voters, the state's billionaires would pay a one-time 5% tax on their accumulated wealth. Revenue from the tax would primarily fund state healthcare programs, with a smaller portion going toward food assistance (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_assistance) and public education. Proposition 40 was sponsored by the labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEIU_United_Healthcare_Workers_West).
Background
Proposition 40 was drafted by tax law professors Brian Galle of UC Berkeley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Berkeley), David Gamage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gamage) of the University of Missouri (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Missouri), Darien Shanske of UC Davis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Davis), and economist Emmanuel Saez (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Saez) of UC Berkeley. [ 1 ] [ 2 ] Labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEIU_United_Healthcare_Workers_West) (SEIU-UHW) filed the initiative. In December 2025, state attorney general Rob Bonta (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Bonta) issued the official title and summary. [ 3 ] [ 4 ]
On April 26, 2026, SEIU-UHW announced that they had collected 1.6 million signatures in support of the tax, nearly double the 874,641 required to qualify for the November ballot. [ 5 ] [ 6 ] On June 17, the California secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) announced that the wealth tax had qualified for the ballot with 980,438 valid signatures. [ 7 ] [ 8 ]
A day later, SEIU-UHW sent a letter to California governor Gavin Newsom (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Newsom)—an opponent of the initiative—offering to withdraw the 5% wealth tax proposal if Newsom supported a smaller 2% levy on billionaires that would

be passed by the state legislature; [ 9 ] [ 10 ] [ 11 ] Newsom quickly rejected the amended proposal. [ 12 ] Negotiations stalled before the June 25 withdrawal deadline, and the initiative was certified for the November ballot. [ 13 ] [ 14 ]
Impact
The initiative would impose the Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the California residents worth over $1 billion. [ 15 ] 90% of revenue from the tax would go towards state-funded healthcare programs, [ 16 ] including Medi-Cal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medi-Cal), while the rest would provide funding for food assistance and public education. [ 15 ]
The eligibility cut-off outlined in Proposition 40 is January 1, 2026, meaning that if the initiative is passed by voters, billionaires who continued to hold residence in the state of California after that date will be subject to the 5% tax. [ 15 ] Seven of the state's estimated 214 billionaires were reported to have left California before or around the deadline, including PayPal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PayPal) co-founder Peter Thiel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel), former Uber (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber) CEO Travis Kalanick (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Kalanick), and Google (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google) co-founders Larry Page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Page) and Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin). [ 17 ] [ 18 ] [ 19 ] They may be subject to a residency audit to determine whether they have sufficiently severed ties with the state. [ 20 ]
Revenue
Analysis by the California Legislative Analyst's Office (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Legislative_Analyst) found the wealth tax was likely to temporarily increase revenue by up to tens of billions of dollars total, collected over several years. [ 21 ] [ 22 ] The analysis also found the tax would possibly decrease income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually from billionaires leaving California. [ 21 ] [ 23 ]
SEIU-UHW, the labor union behind the initiative, estimated that the tax would generate $100 billion, [ 24 ] though revenue from the billionaires who reportedly left the state prior to the deadline accounts for an estimated $29 billion of that sum, according to Fortune (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_(magazine)) . [ 25 ] [ 20 ] Academic Kent Smetters (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_Smetters) cast doubt on SEIU-UHW's estimate, telling the Los Angeles Times (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times) that the union is "not accounting for the different ways that people can move or reclassify wealth". [ 26 ] UC Berkeley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Berkeley) economics professor Enrico Moretti (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Moretti) warned that the tax "has the potential to completely destroy California's economy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California)", and described the revenue estimate as "way overly optimistic." [ 2 ]
The conservative-leaning Hoover Institution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoover_Institution) estimated that "permanent loss of income taxes from the departing residents indicates a high likelihood that net effect of the Billionaire Tax Act will be negative" by almost $25 billion. [ 27 ] This conclusion was criticized by one of the bill's authors, David Gamage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gamage), who contended that the group's analysis "suggests that the billionaire tax might raise more revenue than our projections even say". [ 28 ]
In a guest essay for The New York Times (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times) , Gabriel Zucman (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Zucman) and initiative co-author Saez responded to concerns about billionaires fleeing the state, claiming that because billionaires are able to avoid income tax on most earnings, "even if all of them left the state, it would take 25 years for the loss of their tax payments... to surpass the amount the state would raise" if the initiative passes. [ 29 ] In a working paper (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_paper), Saez and Zucman, alongside co-author Jasper Boll of the Paris School of Economics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_School_of_Economics), estimated that state income tax payments by California billionaires make up 2.4 percent of California's annual income tax revenue. [ 30 ]
Economist Teresa Ghilarducci (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Ghilarducci) of the Economic Policy Institute (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Policy_Institute), a pro-union think tank, considered an exodus of billionaires due to the tax unlikely, pointing to a 2022 Massachusetts 4% surtax (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Massachusetts_Question_1) on income above $1 million that exceeded projected revenue. [ 31 ] Nuveen (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuveen), an asset management company (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asset_management_company), also concluded billionaire outmigration was unlikely and that the tax posed "minimal risk" to California's credit profile and municipal bonds. [ 32 ]
In October 2026, two Stanford University (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University) and Hoover Institution researchers—Benjamin Jaros and Joshua Rauh (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_D._Rauh)—released a working paper that simulated various possible outcomes if Proposition 40 was approved by voters. [ 33 ] The researchers estimated that the proposed tax could cost California $39 billion in tax revenue, with 85 percent of the 100,000 simulated plausible scenarios showing in a net negative revenue impact over the long term. [ 34 ] Emmanuel Saez criticized the revenue estimates in the analysis and its assumption that billionaires would never return to California after the tax. [ 35 ]
Effective tax rate
The Tax Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_Foundation), a center-right think tank, argued that it was possible for the effective wealth tax rate to far exceed 5% for some taxpayers due to provisions related to dual-class share structures, [ 36 ] but acknowledged that this would be unlikely in cases where valuations are clearly incorrect. [ 37 ] [ 38 ] The initiative's drafters published a report arguing that this concern was based on a misreading of the text. [ 37 ] [ 39 ]
Real estate
Forbes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes) cited the billionaire tax initiative as the reason for a real estate boom on Nevada (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada)'s side of Lake Tahoe (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tahoe), noting that a number of lakefront homes were purchased by California billionaires after the proposal was announced. [ 40 ] Bill Dietz, a Lake Tahoe realtor, told the magazine that a "clear acceleration of ultra-high-net-worth buyers moving from California to Nevada" took place, driven by "tax strategy". [ 40 ]
In late 2025, Oracle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_Corporation) founder Larry Ellison (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Ellison) sold his San Francisco (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco) mansion for $45 million, choosing to relocate to Nevada; venture capitalist Steve Jurvetson (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jurvetson) later did the same. [ 41 ] In June 2026, former U.S. ambassador to Kenya (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._ambassador_to_Kenya) Meg Whitman (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meg_Whitman) and her husband, neurosurgeon Griffith R. Harsh (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffith_R._Harsh), sold a number of properties in California, including a $17.9 million fly fishing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly_fishing) ranch, purportedly over fears that the billionaire tax would be approved by voters. [ 41 ]
Campaign
Support
Sanders discussing the billionaire tax in February 2026 Pro-Proposition 40 yard sign in Berkeley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley,_California) Supporters of Proposition 40 at a May 2026 rally
U.S. senator Bernie Sanders (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders), a democratic socialist (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_socialism), has endorsed the billionaire tax. At a February 2026 Los Angeles (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles) rally in support of the tax, Sanders described billionaires as "oligarchs of the 18th century...[who] believe they have the divine right to rule". [ 42 ] Many prominent supporters have asserted that the billionaire tax is a necessary response to the Trump administration (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump)'s restrictions and cuts (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act#Medicaid_restrictions_and_funding_cuts) to Medicaid (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid), [ 43 ] including former U.S. secretary of labor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor) Robert Reich (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Reich), who described the tax as a "practical way to keep the healthcare system functioning". [ 43 ]
The state branch of the Democratic Socialists of America (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Socialists_of_America) endorsed the billionaire tax, stating that "without this funding, thousands of jobs will be lost, millions of Californians could lose coverage altogether, and care facilities across the state could be forced to close". [ 44 ] [ 45 ]
U.S. representative Ro Khanna (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ro_Khanna), a progressive Democrat who represents much of the Silicon Valley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley), has expressed strong support for the tax. [ 46 ] Some venture capitalists from Khanna's district responded by backing his unsuccessful primary challenger (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_California_(districts_1%E2%80%9326)#District_17), Ethan Agarwal. [ 47 ] Two 2026 Democratic gubernatorial candidates, billionaire businessman Tom Steyer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Steyer) and state superintendent of public instruction (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Superintendent_of_Public_Instruction) Tony Thurmond (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Thurmond), endorsed the tax. [ 46 ] [ 48 ]
Current Affairs (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_Affairs_(magazine)) editor Alex Scopic argued in favor of the tax, considering it an important method of countering the "buy, borrow, die (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_avoidance#Buy,_borrow,_die)" tax avoidance strategy by billionaires. [ 38 ] Emmanuel Saez (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Saez), a co-author of the initiative, said that the tax would "preserve [healthcare and education] programs that are crucial for California's economy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California)". [ 2 ]
In August 2026, the California Democratic Party (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Democratic_Party) endorsed Proposition 40. [ 49 ] [ 50 ] After a failed initial endorsement vote and an unsuccessful alternative motion to adopt a neutral position on the measure, a second endorsement vote yielded 61.7 percent in favor, narrowly exceeding the 60 percent threshold for endorsement. [ 51 ]
In September 2026, a group of six progressive Nobel laureates of economics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_laureate_in_economics) published a letter in support of the tax, arguing that it would help address growing inequality in California and loopholes that have allowed billionaires to avoid taxes on capital gains (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_gains_tax). [ 52 ] [ 53 ] [ 54 ] The economists wrote that if California passed Proposition 40, it would "kickstart a movement" to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-net-worth_individual) elsewhere. [ 53 ]
SEIU-UHW extortion and abuse allegations
In February 2026, SEIU United Service Workers West (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEIU) (SEIU-USWW) president David Huerta (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Huerta_(trade_unionist)) and three other labor leaders filed a formal complaint against SEIU-UHW president Dave Regan, accusing him of extorting them by suggesting that he would "report unspecified governance concerns to the U.S. Department of Labor ... if [they] did not support the billionaire tax". [ 55 ] [ 56 ] An investigation initiated by the SEIU's national branch substantiated these claims as well as allegations from SEIU California executive director Tia Orr that Regan had threatened her by telling her to "endorse this measure ... or I'm coming for you". [ 56 ] [ 57 ]
A September 2026 report from SEIU California found that Regan had "engaged in a pattern of subjecting former and current SEIU California female directors to intimidating and threatening physical behavior" and substantiated former union leader Courtni Pugh's allegations that Regan physically assaulted her. [ 56 ] Regan denied this and claimed that because Pugh worked as a political consultant against the tax, she had a reason to lie. [ 56 ] A separate investigation found that Regan had intimidated and bullied SEIU California's government relations director, Jessica Bartholow, by standing "uncomfortably close" to her as "tensions flared over the billionaire tax" before "scream[ing] an expletive at her". [ 56 ]
On September 11, 2026, the California Nurses Association (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Nurses_Association), who support Proposition 40, published a statement urging Regan to resign over "inappropriate, aggressive behavior and threats targeting other labor staff to support the Prop. 40 billionaire tax initiative." [ 58 ] Regan dismissed the allegations as political retaliation over his support for the billionaire tax; an independent investigation found that his claims were unsubstantiated. [ 55 ]
Opposition
California governor Gavin Newsom (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Newsom) has vocally opposed the tax, telling Politico (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico) that the proposal "makes no sense" and is "really damaging to the state". [ 59 ] A number of Democratic candidates who aimed to succeed Newsom in the 2026 gubernatorial election (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_gubernatorial_election) also opposed the tax, including former U.S. representative Katie Porter (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katie_Porter), former U.S. secretary of health and human services (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services) Xavier Becerra (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra), former Los Angeles mayor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_mayor) Antonio Villaraigosa (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Villaraigosa), and San Jose mayor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_San_Jose,_California) Matt Mahan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Mahan). [ 60 ] [ 46 ] Republican (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States)) candidates Chad Bianco (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad_Bianco) and Steve Hilton (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hilton) expressed opposition to the tax. [ 61 ]
Ayn Rand Institute (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayn_Rand_Institute) associate fellow Robertas Bakula argued in the Los Angeles Daily News (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Daily_News) that Proposition 40's eligibility deadline of January 1, 2026, is illegal due to a constitutional ban on retroactive laws (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retroactive_law). [ 62 ] In a February 2026 effort to curb the effects of the eligibility deadline, U.S. representative Kevin Kiley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Kiley_(politician)) introduced a bill in Congress (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress) that would prohibit a state from levying a tax retroactively on people who no longer live in the state. [ 42 ]
In an April 2026 editorial, The Wall Street Journal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal) criticized wording in the act that would allow the state legislature to make amendments that could widen the scope of eligibility for the tax. [ 63 ] In May 2026, The Washington Post (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post) publicly opposed the "self-destructive" tax, stating that the initiative "has already cost the state more in lost future revenue from income taxes than it would raise". [ 64 ] In September 2026, the Los Angeles Times (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times) published its first editorial in 18 months, urging voters to oppose Proposition 40, claiming that it was "poorly drafted" and has "insufficient guardrails to ensure the funds are spent to actually address Californians' most pressing healthcare needs". [ 65 ] In a later interview, former Los Angeles Times editor Mariel Garza noted that the newspaper's owner, Patrick Soon-Shiong (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Soon-Shiong), is a billionaire. [ 66 ]
Google co-founder Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin) has spent more than $100 million opposing the tax
Building a Better California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_a_Better_California), an organization co-founded by Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin) and Eric Schmidt (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Schmidt) that is opposed to the billionaire tax, [ 67 ] introduced two questions to the November 2026 ballot, which are designed to curb the effects of the billionaire tax if it passes. [ 68 ] [ 16 ] One, known as Proposition 41, would bar new taxes from circumventing rules on education spending requirements for tax revenue, [ 69 ] [ 68 ] while Proposition 42 would invalidate the billionaire tax by amending the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) to forbid retroactive taxation. [ 68 ] [ 70 ] Another measure that would have required more audits of special taxes and imposed more rules on how revenue could be spent did not qualify for the ballot. [ 71 ] [ 42 ]
By August 2026, Building a Better California had raised $118 million, primarily from Brin, Chris Larsen (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Larsen), and John Doerr (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Doerr). [ 72 ] [ 73 ] [ 74 ] Peter Thiel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel) has separately contributed around $100 million to an anti-Proposition 40 committee led by the California Business Roundtable (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Business_Roundtable?action=edit&redlink=1). [ 75 ]
Dozens of anti-Proposition 40 protestors staged a "pro-billionaire" march (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_for_Billionaires) in San Francisco (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco) on February 7, 2026. [ 76 ]
In June 2026, a number of progressive organizations [ 77 ] [ 78 ] announced their opposition to the billionaire tax. [ 79 ] [ 80 ] [ 81 ] In a joint statement, Planned Parenthood (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood) and the California Medical Association (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Medical_Association) criticized the wealth tax's ambiguity and described it as a "flawed response" to health care cuts, [ 79 ] while the California Teachers Association (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Teachers_Association) stated that the billionaire tax "will not provide the sustainable and long-lasting funding that our schools and communities deserve". [ 81 ] That same month, various California housing advocacy groups—including California YIMBY (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_YIMBY)—opposed the tax, fearing that it would discourage investment and worsen the state's housing shortage. [ 82 ]
Several California labor unions have opposed Proposition 40, [ 79 ] arguing that the measure contains a loophole that would allow the state legislature to tax the savings and retirement accounts of all residents. Opponents say its passage would undercut state tax revenues in the long run and stifle innovation as many of California's highest paying taxpayers and most successful individuals may choose to leave the state to avoid the tax.
